$comment: The Part II lookup appendix. NOT a lesson and NOT part of the progression — it is reference, it is not numbered, and it must never be fed to buildDeck. Every row carries a provenance status; anything whose standing could not be established was dropped rather than guessed, which is why this is shorter than the source.
$provenance: These rows were transcribed from a secondary source that cites the January 2025 multi-service brevity publication. Nobody on this project has opened the primary publication — it is not reachable from here — so every 'multi-service' row should be read as 'a transcription says so', not as first-hand. Brevity definitions move between editions, which is why the edition is named at all.

categories.title: Engagement regimes
categories.note: Where a fight is happening and which skill set is being exercised there.

categories.title: Intercept phases
categories.note: The five-phase public model of how an intercept unfolds, from building the picture to what happens after the merge.

categories.title: BVR timeline and decisions
categories.note: The calls that mark points on a beyond-visual-range timeline: who owns which target, when a weapon is away, and when to leave.

categories.title: Individual BVR manoeuvres
categories.note: Single-aircraft manoeuvres and geometry flown before the merge, each one a way of trading closure, angles or radar support.

categories.title: BVR engagement flows
categories.note: Prebriefed whole-engagement plans that settle what happens after the missile comes off the rail.

categories.title: Friendly formations
categories.note: How friendly fighters arrange themselves relative to one another.

categories.title: Tactical picture labels
categories.note: Labels describing how detected groups are arranged on the scope, not how friendlies are flying.

categories.title: Multi-ship tactics
categories.note: Tactics and roles for two or more friendly fighters working the same problem.

categories.title: BFM concepts
categories.note: The geometry, pursuit and energy ideas that explain why close-in manoeuvres work.

categories.title: Named BFM manoeuvres
categories.note: Manoeuvres flown to solve a range, angles or closure problem in a visual fight.

categories.title: Counter-missile calls
categories.note: Calls and considerations for when a radar-guided weapon is the problem.

categories.title: Air-to-air brevity words
categories.note: Standard radio words for identifying, describing and reporting what is out there.

terms.means: The part of an engagement fought before the aircraft can see each other, so it names a range regime rather than a tactic.
terms.confusedWith: ACT, which is a kind of tactical employment usually carried out in BVR, not the regime it happens in

terms.means: The part of an engagement fought once the aircraft can see each other and visual manoeuvring decides the outcome.
terms.confusedWith: BFM, which is a skill set exercised inside this regime rather than the regime itself

terms.means: The point at which friendly and target aircraft have arrived in the visual arena.
terms.confusedWith: WVR, which is the whole regime, whereas the merge is the single moment of entry into it

terms.means: The piece of sky the fight has arrived in after the merge, which does not by itself mean everyone has seen everyone.
terms.confusedWith: WVR, which names the regime as a category, whereas the visual arena is the specific environment the aircraft are now in

terms.means: The one-versus-one skill set of geometry, energy management and weapons positioning, solved live against range, angles and closure rather than run off a list of set-piece moves.
terms.confusedWith: ACM, which sets the same geometry problems inside a formation where mutual support also has to be solved

terms.means: Element-level air-to-air manoeuvring, which adds a second friendly aircraft and the problem of staying mutually supporting to the BFM skill set.
terms.confusedWith: BFM, which is the same problem one-versus-one with no wingman to deconflict from

terms.means: Element-level air-to-air employment carried out primarily beyond visual range.
terms.confusedWith: ACM, which is the manoeuvring itself rather than the employment plan the element is flying

terms.means: The phase spent building the picture and holding position while deciding whether the situation meets the briefed criteria to start an intercept.
terms.confusedWith: the idea that nothing tactical has begun, when the information gathering that drives the commit decision happens here
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: The phase after the fighters have committed, while the intercept develops towards a firing solution.
terms.confusedWith: weapons employment, which is the later phase in which the missile actually comes off the rail
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: The phase in which targeting and sort responsibilities are settled and missiles are fired.
terms.confusedWith: the merge, which is a separate later phase and only happens if the engagement continues that far
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: The phase in which friendly and threat aircraft enter the visual arena.
terms.confusedWith: becoming offensive or defensive, which the merge settles nothing about on its own
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: The phase after the merge, in which fighters clear, continue, support, separate or transition into visual manoeuvring.
terms.confusedWith: BFM, which is only one of the ways this phase can go, since the engagement may simply end
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Begin an intercept against the group of interest according to the criteria briefed beforehand.
terms.confusedWith: PRESS, which approves continuing an action already under way rather than starting the intercept

terms.means: Assign responsibility for a group to a particular fighter.
terms.confusedWith: SORT, which divides responsibility among contacts inside one group rather than handing out whole groups

terms.means: The fighter has acquired its assigned group and taken responsibility for it.
terms.confusedWith: a radar lock, which is a sensor state and not the assumption of responsibility that TARGETED reports

terms.means: Allocate responsibility for the individual contacts within a single group.
terms.confusedWith: TARGET, which allocates responsibility at the level of whole groups rather than inside one

terms.means: The sort responsibilities have been satisfied.
terms.confusedWith: TARGETED, which reports responsibility for a whole group rather than the division of contacts inside it

terms.means: An air-to-air weapon has been launched, actually or in simulation.
terms.confusedWith: a hit, which is reported separately, and the missile going active, which is a later call in the timeline

terms.means: The active-radar missile has reached its high pulse repetition frequency active range.
terms.confusedWith: PITBULL, which is the later medium PRF active range point on the same missile's timeline

terms.means: The active-radar missile has reached its medium pulse repetition frequency active range.
terms.confusedWith: the blanket claim that the shooter is now free to leave, which depends on the weapon and the geometry rather than on the call itself

terms.means: Turn to a cold aspect relative to the known threat, as launch-and-leave tactics require.
terms.confusedWith: BUGOUT, which ends the engagement outright, whereas OUT is a turn within a plan that may still continue

terms.means: The requested action is approved and mutual support will be maintained; the air-to-air meaning assumes visual.
terms.confusedWith: BANZAI, which is a launch-and-decide flow the shooter executes rather than an approval granted to someone else

terms.means: Separate from the engagement with no intention of returning or re-engaging.
terms.confusedWith: EXTEND, which buys distance and energy with the intention of coming back

terms.means: Return and reorganise according to the tactical plan so another engagement opportunity can be set up.
terms.confusedWith: BUGOUT, which abandons the engagement rather than reorganising for a second attempt

terms.means: Turn laterally while holding the target near the radar gimbal limits, which cuts closure without giving up radar support.
terms.confusedWith: F-pole, which is a distance metric and not a manoeuvre, though cranking is often flown to improve it

terms.means: Put the threat roughly on the 3-9 line, which brevity uses as a contact aspect and pilots use as geometry to fly.
terms.confusedWith: notch, since beam names an aspect and not the doppler rejection that beam geometry is usually flown to achieve

terms.means: Manoeuvre defensively with reference to a threat, in practice arranging low radial velocity so a doppler radar rejects the return, often helped by ground clutter, altitude change and chaff.
terms.confusedWith: beam, since every successful doppler notch uses beam-like geometry but beaming alone does not guarantee the rejection

terms.means: In brevity, a contact pointing generally away; in tactical conversation, deliberately drawing a threat away.
terms.confusedWith: OUT, which directs a turn to cold, whereas drag describes the aspect a contact already presents

terms.means: Manoeuvre in a specified direction relative to the target.
terms.confusedWith: crank, which is the narrower case of displacing while pinning the target at the radar gimbal limit

terms.means: Fly geometry that cuts across where the target is going instead of chasing where it has been.
terms.confusedWith: lead pursuit, which is a pursuit curve inside a turning fight rather than an intercept geometry flown at range

terms.means: Fly the briefed manoeuvre that minimises closure with the threat or a boundary, with the intention of turning back in.
terms.confusedWith: BUGOUT, which leaves for good; the multi-service meaning also differs from the NATO one

terms.means: Temporarily gain energy, distance or separation with the intention of re-engaging.
terms.confusedWith: BUGOUT, which separates with no intention of returning

terms.means: Turn immediately at maximum performance in the direction commanded.
terms.confusedWith: an ordinary defensive turn, which is not the maximum-performance response a break demands

terms.means: Reverse heading with the nose high.
terms.confusedWith: a slice, which reverses nose-low and descending rather than over the top

terms.means: Reverse with a high-G descending turn.
terms.confusedWith: a split-S, which is a half-roll pulled through the vertical rather than a descending turn

terms.means: Manoeuvre unpredictably to spoil an opponent's tracking solution.
terms.confusedWith: a break, which is one maximum-performance turn rather than a sequence whose value is its unpredictability

terms.means: Alter the intercept flow so that interaction with a separate tactical group is avoided or managed.
terms.confusedWith: a crank, which is flown to hold radar support on the group being engaged rather than to hold a different group off

terms.means: Execute the prebriefed launch-and-leave tactic at the briefed range: shoot, then separate instead of pressing to the merge.
terms.confusedWith: crank, which is a single manoeuvre inside an engagement rather than a whole prebriefed flow

terms.means: A modifier of SKATE rather than a manoeuvre of its own, setting a closer briefed range and timeline for the launch-and-leave.
terms.confusedWith: a closer crank, which it is not, since the range and timeline come from the brief attached to the SKATE call

terms.means: A modifier of SKATE setting a longer briefed launch-and-leave range and timeline.
terms.confusedWith: the idea that SKATE has one fixed range, when the range is exactly what the modifier sets

terms.means: A third recognised modifier of SKATE, whose execution is defined by the mission brief or TTP.
terms.confusedWith: Short Skate, which is a different modifier of the same call with its own briefed range

terms.means: Execute the launch-and-decide tactic: shoot, then keep manoeuvring towards the visual arena if the briefed criteria support it.
terms.confusedWith: pressing regardless of the situation, when the whole point is a decision measured against briefed criteria after the shot

terms.means: Two fighters fly roughly side by side so each can look through the other's blind areas and cover the other's tail.
terms.confusedWith: WALL, which is a picture label for three or more detected groups spread in azimuth and says nothing about how anyone is flying

terms.means: Wingmen sit aft of and offset from the lead, giving the lead room to manoeuvre while the wingman holds position.
terms.confusedWith: the same word used as a picture label, where it describes detected contacts rather than your own flight

terms.means: The wingman holds a manoeuvring cone behind and to the side of the lead, following through hard turns instead of holding one fixed line.
terms.confusedWith: parade or route position, which is a close non-manoeuvring formation flown for transit rather than for fighting

terms.means: A loose two-ship formation in which the wingman has wide latitude in position so both aircraft can manoeuvre freely.
terms.confusedWith: Loose Deuce, which is a historical mutual-support tactic about who may become the attacker rather than a formation geometry

terms.means: Aircraft fly one behind the other, separated mainly in range rather than across the sky.
terms.confusedWith: LEAD-TRAIL, which describes two detected groups separated in range and is a picture term, not a friendly formation

terms.means: Two detected groups separated mainly side to side across your nose.
terms.confusedWith: line abreast, which is a friendly formation rather than a description of how contacts are arranged
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Two detected groups separated mainly in depth, one behind the other.
terms.confusedWith: trail formation, which is how friendly aircraft are flying rather than how contacts are arranged
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Three or more detected groups spread mainly in azimuth.
terms.confusedWith: a friendly line-abreast formation; WALL says how the groups appear in the tactical picture, not that those aircraft are flying any particular formation
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Three or more detected groups stacked in range, one behind the other.
terms.confusedWith: trail formation, which describes friendly aircraft rather than detected groups
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Three detected groups arranged so that azimuth and range separation combine in a defined relationship.
terms.confusedWith: VIC, the other three-group picture, which places the single group at the opposite end of the arrangement
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Three detected groups with one group leading and two groups trailing it in range and separated in azimuth.
terms.confusedWith: CHAMPAGNE, which is also a three-group picture but with the single group at the other end
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Four detected groups arranged as two lead groups and two trail groups.
terms.confusedWith: a four-ship box formation, which describes your own aircraft rather than the contacts on the scope
terms.src: Multi-service Air Control Communication TTP, October 2024

terms.means: Vertical separation between the contacts held inside a single group.
terms.confusedWith: a friendly high/low split, which is friendlies deliberately separating in altitude rather than a description of contacts

terms.means: Friendly fighters manoeuvre to opposite sides of the target, laterally or vertically, so the target cannot solve both at once.
terms.confusedWith: PINCE, which describes a threat manoeuvring to bracket YOU rather than your own attack

terms.means: A call that the threat is manoeuvring to bracket you.
terms.confusedWith: BRACKET, which is the same geometry flown by friendlies against the target rather than flown against you

terms.means: A loose general description of converging pressure applied from opposed axes.
terms.confusedWith: BRACKET and PINCE, which are precise brevity words with assigned meanings, whereas pincer gets used loosely for either and should not be treated as equivalent to either

terms.means: Formation members deliberately separate when attacked so the attacker must choose one, opening a chance for the other to come back on him.
terms.confusedWith: the brevity word SPLIT, which means a flight member leaving to press a separate attack, not a reaction to being attacked

terms.means: A flight member is leaving the formation to pursue a separate attack, and visual contact may not be maintained.
terms.confusedWith: a defensive split, which is an informal label for a defensive reaction rather than this offensive departure from formation

terms.means: The fighter actively manoeuvring against the threat, who relinquishes normal deconfliction responsibility to do it.
terms.confusedWith: the flight lead, since either aircraft can be the engaged fighter regardless of who leads the formation

terms.means: The fighter holding a position from which it can influence the outcome, and which carries the deconfliction responsibility.
terms.confusedWith: merely being nearby, whereas SUPPORTING asserts a position that can actually change the fight

terms.means: A two-aircraft mutual-support scheme from the Vietnam era in which either fighter may take over as the attacker as the fight develops.
terms.confusedWith: the modern engaged and supporting contract, which assigns those roles explicitly rather than letting them pass back and forth by opportunity

terms.means: One aircraft draws an opponent into a chase while another exploits the geometry that creates.
terms.confusedWith: the brevity word DRAG, which describes a contact pointing away from you and carries no implication of a two-ship plan

terms.means: Fighters take turns pressing and then falling back to reset while others take over the pressure.
terms.confusedWith: SKATE, which is a briefed launch-and-leave call rather than a repeating cycle shared between aircraft

terms.means: Opposing aircraft have ended up on both sides of you.
terms.confusedWith: BRACKET, which is the same shape but flown deliberately by friendlies against a target rather than suffered

terms.means: You start with the positional advantage and work to keep it long enough to turn it into a shot.
terms.confusedWith: having the energy advantage, since the attacker often has less energy and is managing an overshoot problem instead

terms.means: You start at a positional disadvantage and deny the attacker a solution while looking for an escape or a reversal.
terms.confusedWith: missile defence, which is about defeating one specific weapon rather than solving the whole positional problem

terms.means: Both fighters arrive at large aspect with neither holding a rear-quarter advantage.
terms.confusedWith: the word neutral, which suggests the two are exactly equal when in practice one usually holds some edge in energy or nose position

terms.means: How the target is oriented relative to you, measured from its tail round to your position.
terms.confusedWith: heading crossing angle, which measures the difference between the two headings rather than the target's orientation to you

terms.means: The angular difference between your heading and the target's heading.
terms.confusedWith: aspect angle, which is measured from the target's tail to you and can be very different from the heading difference

terms.means: You point ahead of where the target is now, which cuts across its path and builds closure.
terms.confusedWith: a lead turn, which is a manoeuvre begun before the pass rather than one of the three pursuit curves

terms.means: You point your nose directly at the target.
terms.confusedWith: a collision-course lead, which points ahead of the target to meet it rather than at where it currently is

terms.means: You point behind the target, which bleeds off closure and buys room to solve the angles.
terms.confusedWith: an extension, which is separating from the fight entirely with intent to return, whereas lag stays inside the turn

terms.means: How quickly you change heading.
terms.confusedWith: turn radius, which is how much sky the turn consumes rather than how fast the nose comes round

terms.means: How much sky your turn takes up.
terms.confusedWith: turn rate, since a fast turn is not automatically a tight one and the two trade against each other with speed

terms.means: The speed region where the G limit and the lift limit meet, giving the best available turn performance for that aircraft and configuration.
terms.confusedWith: best sustained-rate speed, which is about holding a turn indefinitely rather than peaking it, and is usually a different number

terms.means: Your combined speed and altitude, which is what you actually have to spend on manoeuvring.
terms.confusedWith: airspeed alone, which ignores the altitude you can trade back into speed

terms.means: The displacement available for you to turn in before your flightpath conflicts with the opponent's.
terms.confusedWith: raw separation, since range directly behind an opponent with no lateral or vertical offset gives you nothing to turn in

terms.means: The region behind an opponent from which you can hold an offensive position rather than sliding out of it.
terms.confusedWith: a weapon envelope, which is where a shot is valid rather than where sustained control is possible; the exact definition also varies by syllabus and platform

terms.means: The fighters turn in opposite directions after the pass and share one common turning circle.
terms.confusedWith: the rule that it is always a radius fight, when radius tends to dominate but does not decide the outcome by itself

terms.means: The fighters turn in the same relative direction after the pass, each on its own circle.
terms.confusedWith: the rule that it is always a rate fight, when rate tends to dominate but does not decide the outcome by itself

terms.means: The attacker's flightpath crosses the defender's flightpath.
terms.confusedWith: a 3/9-line overshoot, which is about passing forward of the defender's wingline and can cost you the advantage outright

terms.means: The attacker slides forward of the defender's wingline, which can hand the positional advantage over.
terms.confusedWith: a flightpath overshoot, which crosses the defender's path without necessarily giving up position

terms.means: You begin turning before passing the opponent so the available turning room gets used instead of wasted.
terms.confusedWith: lead pursuit, which is where your nose points during a chase rather than when you start the turn

terms.means: An immediate maximum-performance turn in the direction called.
terms.confusedWith: any hard defensive turn, whereas BREAK directs everything the aircraft has, right now

terms.means: You trade speed for height and pull the nose across, killing excess closure while holding onto the angles.
terms.confusedWith: a pure vertical manoeuvre, since a high yo-yo mostly stays in the plane of the fight and comes straight back down into position

terms.means: You drop below the opponent's plane to trade height for speed and cut the corner back into position.
terms.confusedWith: simply diving for speed, which gains energy but does nothing about the geometry

terms.means: A three-dimensional roll flown around the opponent's flightpath to burn off closure without surrendering the position.
terms.confusedWith: the aerobatic barrel roll, which is a display manoeuvre with no opponent to reference

terms.means: An out-of-plane roll that moves you sideways off the opponent's flightpath to create turning room.
terms.confusedWith: the barrel-roll attack, which is flown around the opponent rather than to displace away from his path, and with a plain roll about the longitudinal axis

terms.means: An out-of-plane lag manoeuvre used to handle a flightpath overshoot that a simple lag pull cannot fix.
terms.confusedWith: a high yo-yo, which attacks the same closure problem but stays largely in the plane of the turn

terms.means: Both fighters reverse back and forth in the horizontal, each trying to force the other out in front.
terms.confusedWith: rolling scissors, which fights the same battle through the vertical rather than flat on the deck

terms.means: Both fighters roll over and around each other through the vertical, trading who is ahead as they go.
terms.confusedWith: flat scissors, which is the horizontal version and rewards different aircraft qualities

terms.means: You change the direction of your turn, usually to exploit an overshoot or a change in geometry.
terms.confusedWith: a scissors, which is a repeated series of reversals by both aircraft rather than one change of direction

terms.means: You separate to buy back distance and energy, meaning to come back into the fight.
terms.confusedWith: BUGOUT, which is leaving with no intention of returning at all

terms.means: You push off the G so the aircraft stops bleeding energy and accelerates.
terms.confusedWith: diving, which trades height for speed, whereas unloading simply stops paying the drag bill

terms.means: You carry on through the merge rather than staying to fight the same opponent.
terms.confusedWith: an extension, which is a temporary separation flown with the intent to re-engage the same fight

terms.means: You are manoeuvring defensively with reference to a radar threat.
terms.confusedWith: DEFENSIVE, which says the further thing that you can no longer assure deconfliction or mutual support

terms.means: You are under attack, manoeuvring defensively, and cannot assure normal deconfliction or mutual support.
terms.confusedWith: DEFENDING, which is the lesser state where you are still holding up your side of the formation contract

terms.means: A reminder to set the throttles with the infrared threat and your energy state in mind.
terms.confusedWith: flare deployment, which releases a countermeasure rather than changing your own signature and energy

terms.means: A described sequence of separating from the threat and then setting beam-like geometry against its radar.
terms.confusedWith: a formally named manoeuvre, when this is descriptive shorthand rather than anything briefed or published

terms.means: An air contact whose identity is not known.
terms.confusedWith: BANDIT, which is a contact positively identified as an enemy; a bogey has not been identified at all

terms.means: An aircraft positively identified as an enemy under the theatre identification criteria.
terms.confusedWith: clearance to shoot, which BANDIT does not grant on its own

terms.means: A track that meets the applicable criteria for hostile identification and engagement.
terms.confusedWith: BANDIT, which identifies an enemy aircraft without the engagement criteria having been satisfied

terms.means: Contacts held close enough together that the grouping criteria treat them as one entity.
terms.confusedWith: a flight of aircraft, since a group is what the sensors resolve and may contain a different number of jets than you assume

terms.means: A single sensor return, with the sensor and the context determining what it actually means.
terms.confusedWith: a visually acquired aircraft, which is reported as TALLY or VISUAL rather than as a sensor contact

terms.means: A request for the tactical situation laid out in group terms.
terms.confusedWith: asking what is on someone's radar, since PICTURE asks for the built tactical situation rather than raw returns

terms.means: A contact's bearing, range, altitude and aspect measured from a named friendly aircraft.
terms.confusedWith: a BULLSEYE call, which is measured from a fixed common reference point instead of from an aircraft

terms.means: An agreed reference point that everyone measures bearing and range from.
terms.confusedWith: BRAA, which is measured from one specific friendly aircraft and so means different things to different listeners

terms.means: A request for information on the nearest or specified group, given in BRAA format.
terms.confusedWith: DECLARE, which asks who a track is rather than where it is

terms.means: A request for the identification of a specified track or group.
terms.confusedWith: a request to engage, which DECLARE is not; it only asks who that is

terms.means: You have the target, bandit or enemy position in sight.
terms.confusedWith: VISUAL, which is sighting a friendly aircraft rather than the enemy

terms.means: You do not have the target or bandit in sight.
terms.confusedWith: BLIND, which is losing sight of a friendly rather than of the enemy

terms.means: You have a friendly aircraft or position in sight.
terms.confusedWith: TALLY, which is sighting the enemy rather than a friendly

terms.means: You have lost sight of the friendly aircraft or position.
terms.confusedWith: NO JOY, which is not seeing the enemy rather than not seeing your own side

terms.means: Your warning receiver shows an airborne interceptor radar tracking or launching on you.
terms.confusedWith: NAILS, which is the same kind of radar merely searching rather than holding you

terms.means: Your warning receiver shows an airborne interceptor radar in search, not tracking you.
terms.confusedWith: SPIKE, which means that radar has you in track or is launching

terms.means: A valid weapons effect has been observed on the target.
terms.confusedWith: a FOX call, which announces a launch and says nothing about the result

terms.means: You have no ordnance remaining at all.
terms.confusedWith: SKOSH, which is only about active-radar missiles and leaves your other weapons unaccounted for

terms.means: You are out of, or unable to employ, active-radar missiles.
terms.confusedWith: WINCHESTER, which means no weapons of any kind remain
